# The Lantern Maker's Daughter

The shop had stood in the same corner of Chang'an for three hundred years, though no one remembered when it was built. Its wooden sign, painted with fading red lanterns, creaked in the autumn wind.

I inherited it from my uncle in the year of the Iron Rat, inheriting also his debts and his secrets—though I didn't know about the secrets then.

The first time I saw her, I thought she was a customer.

She appeared one evening as violet twilight settled over the city. I was preparing the shop for closing, hanging paper lanterns from the ceiling beams—delicate things with patterns of cranes and clouds. A woman in a pale green robe watched from the threshold, her movements so still she might have been another lantern, waiting to be lit.

"We close at dusk," I said, not unkindly.

"I know," she replied. Her voice carried the hollow sound of wind through empty rooms. "I have always come at dusk."

She moved deeper into the shop without waiting for permission. Her fingers trailed along the workbenches where I shaped bamboo frames and stretched paper thin as skin. She picked up a half-finished lantern, examining it with an intensity that made my neck prickle.

"You do it differently than he did," she said. "Your father."

"My uncle raised me. My father died when I was a child."

"Yes." She set down the lantern with great care. "He died. I remember."

Something in her tone made me study her more closely. She couldn't have been more than thirty, yet her eyes held the weight of ages. Her skin had an odd translucence, as if lit from within.

"Who are you?" I asked.

"Someone who used to buy lanterns here. Someone who used to stand where you stand now." She smiled, and I saw sadness in it like depths in water. "My name was Mei. I will always be Mei."

She came again the next evening, and the next. Always at dusk, always silent except for rare, cryptic words. She never bought anything. Instead, she would watch me work and sometimes touch the completed lanterns with reverence, as if they were sacred objects.

My customers began to notice her.

"Who is that woman?" asked Old Chen, who bought lanterns for his restaurant. "I've never seen her before, but she seems familiar somehow."

"A regular customer," I lied, though I knew nothing of the sort.

One night, my uncle's account books fell open in my lap—I had finally begun organizing the shop's finances. Tucked between the pages was a journal entry in my uncle's spidery hand, dated forty years prior:

*Mei came to the shop today, as she does every evening. She never ages. She never buys anything. When I asked her why she comes, she wept—the first time I've seen tears from her. She said she comes to remember what it felt like to be alive. I think I understand now why my brother never spoke of her, why he left this shop to me with such urgency. Some debts cannot be repaid in money.*

The entry ended abruptly, the next page torn away.

That night, I didn't close the shop. I waited for her in the darkness, surrounded by hanging lanterns that glowed softly in the starlight filtering through the windows.

She came as always, but this time she seemed less substantial, as if she were made of the same paper as my lanterns.

"You've read the journals," she said. It wasn't a question.

"Tell me," I whispered.

She sat on my work stool, and I noticed she didn't quite rest her weight upon it—she hovered, barely touching.

"I was the lantern maker's daughter," Mei began. "Your father's sister, though not by blood. He found me abandoned as an infant and raised me as his own. I was happy here, in this shop, among the light and color. I learned the craft. I had dreams of marrying the merchant's son." 

She paused, her voice growing thin. "One evening, a fire broke out in the warehouse where oil was stored. Your father went in to save the lanterns he'd made—such beautiful things, he said, mustn't let them burn. I followed. I was foolish and brave and in love, and I thought I could help."

"What happened?" I asked, though I already knew.

"The roof fell. He got out. I didn't." She looked at her translucent hands. "But I lingered. I didn't know why at first. There was something unfinished in me, some attachment to this place, to the beauty we made here. Your father—he understood. He didn't run screaming when I appeared. He continued his work, and my presence seemed to comfort him somehow. We were bound together by guilt and loss and lanterns."

"Why do you stay?" I asked.

"Because," Mei said softly, "every lantern that leaves this shop carries light into the darkness. Every festival, every celebration, every remembrance of the dead—people gather around light from this place. And in that light, I feel less dead. As long as someone tends this shop with care and love, as long as beautiful lanterns are made here, I am not entirely forgotten. I am not entirely gone."

She stood, and in the lantern light, I could see through her to the wall behind.

"Your uncle understood this. So do you, I think. You remake the lanterns not quite the same way each time—you add your own touches. Your own light."

"What happens if the shop closes?" I asked, terrified of the answer.

"Then I will fade completely. I will become as forgotten as dust. Your father feared this. Your uncle feared this. Now you know why this place must continue, why it is never truly just a shop."

I kept the lantern shop open. I worked harder than I ever had, perfecting the craft, adding innovations, creating designs no one had attempted before. The shop prospered as it never had under my uncle's care.

And Mei continued to visit every evening at dusk.

But something changed. As the shop flourished, her visits grew shorter, her form more substantial. One evening, I realized I could no longer see through her.

"You're fading anyway," I said, not bothering to hide my sorrow.

"No," she smiled—and it was a true smile now, free of the terrible sadness that had haunted it. "I'm finally at peace. Your love for this craft, for this place—it has completed what your father began. I'm not bound anymore. I can let go."

She came one last time on the autumn evening of the Mid-Autumn Festival. The city was ablaze with lanterns—thousands of them, many bearing my marks. The sky itself seemed to glow with light.

"Look," she said, pointing out the window.

"I see," I whispered.

"I can go now." She turned to me, and I saw tears on her cheeks—real tears, the tears of someone moving toward peace. "Thank you for keeping the light burning. Thank you for remembering me, even though you never knew me. Tell your children about this place. Tell them about the lanterns. Tell them about Mei, who loved beauty and light."

"I will," I promised.

She faded like lantern light at dawn, not suddenly but gently, dissolving into the gathering dark until there was nothing left but the faint scent of paper and bamboo, and the sound of wind chimes that had no reason to chime.

The lantern shop stands on that same corner still. I am old now, and my children run it as I taught them. Every evening at dusk, we light the lanterns in the windows—a habit I've never quite explained to them, though they never questioned it.

Sometimes, visitors remark that the shop feels peaceful, that it carries a spirit of its own. On autumn evenings, when the light is just right, they sometimes report seeing a translucent figure among the paper lanterns, smiling peacefully as if she has finally found what she was looking for.

And perhaps she has.

For as long as the lanterns burn, she is remembered. And while she is remembered, she is not truly gone.
